Stage 2 · Physics + sensors · Simulated test world: 579 wells, two datasets

A model that separates the water from the sensor.

A borewell sensor never reports the water table directly. It reports a level taken minutes or hours after the pump stopped, from an instrument that can drift, jump or freeze. This model keeps the true level as a hidden quantity, describes separately how the water moves and how the sensor gets it wrong, and corrects its estimate with every new reading.

The idea

Two equations instead of one: one for the water, one for the sensor. The filter keeps them honest with each other.

  1. Inputs. Terrain from public maps sets each well's starting guess; city rain arrives after delays of 5–150 days; own pumping and neighbours' pumping (within 1.5 km) deepen the level.
  2. The true level, hidden. It drifts back toward normal at a learned pace, rises with rain, falls with pumping, and follows a trend and a yearly cycle.
  3. What the sensor reports. The true level plus drawdown left over from the last pumping, plus any offset, drift or stuck value (checked against the pump's power), plus noise.
  4. Correction. Each new reading corrects the estimate of the true level (Kalman filter).

Three layers

Each layer handles one way a reading can mislead. Each can be switched off, so its worth can be measured.

Layer 1

Sensor faults

Pumps give a second, independent depth gauge: the power a pump draws per litre it lifts grows with the depth it lifts from. Every level reading is checked against it. A level sensor that drifts, jumps or freezes disagrees with the pump, and the disagreement is measured and removed. Impossible values, outliers and frozen readings are dropped first.

Removing this layer raises the error on faulty-sensor wells from 1.11 m to 2.68 m.

Layer 2

Readings taken too early

Half of all readings are taken 8 to 16 hours after the pump last stopped, often before the well has fully recovered. Each well's recovery curve, a fast part and a slow part, is learned from pairs of sessions, and each start reading is corrected for the drawdown still left in it.

Removing this layer raises the nowcast error from 0.52 m to 0.63 m; it helps most on ridge wells and slightly hurts the fastest valley wells.

Layer 3

How the water moves

Day by day, the true level drifts back toward normal, rises with rain arriving through four delays (about 5, 20, 60 and 150 days, with heavy rain treated separately), falls with the well's own and its neighbours' pumping, and follows a slow trend and a yearly cycle. Each well has about 20 settings, fitted from three years of its own data.

This is what carries the forecast beyond a month: the cleaned reading held flat is 1.22 m off at 12 weeks, the model 0.74 m.

The equations, compared with the earlier model

The earlier outlook was one weekly equation fitted to the readings. The new model has two equations, one for the hidden level and one for the sensor, and takes each well's settings from terrain when it has no history. Depths are metres below ground: a larger number is deeper.

pumping, rain in four lag windows (each only allowed to raise the level), a yearly cycle

the sensor: leftover drawdown after Δt hours off, sensor bias b (from the pump-power check), noise

The test world

Testing a model that separates truth from readings needs a world where the truth is known. We built one, then built the model without looking at it.

Dataset A

579 wells, five hidden types

Valley or ridge, weathered or fractured rock, and low-yield wells, placed by terrain. Five years (2021–2026) after a two-year settling run, driven by real NASA rainfall. Percolation through paved ground, harvesting pits and drains, pipe leakage, lakes, and neighbours that affect each other. 1.8 million sessions, 43 million telemetry rows, faults on 10 % of wells.

Dataset B

Built differently, on purpose

Every trait range scaled by an independent factor of 0.8–1.25, twice as many in-between wells, a different geography and pumping behaviour. The model was never tuned on it: every setting chosen on A was applied to B once. A method that only works on the world it was built for is exposed here.

Public-quality maps

Imperfect maps, like real ones

The model never sees the simulator's terrain. It gets maps degraded the way public maps are: elevation with 2 m of error and roofs in it, about 60 % of fracture lines mapped and shifted, false lines added, paved share and drains with gaps. See the maps →

How it was tested honestly

Plan firstMethod, scoring and the expected results written down and fingerprinted (SHA-256) on 30 September 2026 at 06:52 UTC, before any model ran. Changes loggedEight changes before scoring, each with its reason and what had been seen: for example, making the fault correction look only backwards in time, and fixing a bug that pinned some settings to zero. FirewallThe model code never reads the answer key; a test checks it. Only the map maker and the scorer may. SplitSettings fitted on August 2021 – July 2024; band widths set on the next year using the model's own data only; test year August 2025 – July 2026, forecast every Sunday, scored once. Unseen wells116 wells never fitted: their settings come from terrain alone. BaselinesThe latest rested reading held flat; a seasonal guess; the model's own cleaned reading held flat.
Honest status
  • All of this is on simulated wells we built ourselves. The model's water balance is from the same textbook family as the simulator's, so these scores are an upper bound for the field.
  • The pump-power check is idealised in the simulator (clean meters, no pipe friction or pump wear).
  • The map errors are our assumptions about public maps.
  • Slow ridge and low-yield wells are still read about 1 m too deep, and the uncertainty bands are too narrow. Why →
  • The simulated datasets are awaiting a hydrologist's review; if they change, the model is rerun.
Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: vendor export (15 days, July 2026, in the vendor's real format but with demonstration water-level values), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (a physics-based simulation of the 579 wells over a year). No real water-level measurement has been used yet, and nothing here is yet a validated field forecast.
